comments.name: Oops

Some women have the "menopause" symptoms described in this article for less than one year,  and others for more than a decade. 

 NYT does not mention this difference or the reason but should.  It is not genetic.  The women with just a few months of hot flashes usually used pads during their periods; while those with years of hot flashes used tampons.  

Using a tampon delays the excretion of menstrual blood until the tampon is removed, during which time the high level of carbon monoxide in menstrual blood is absorbed into surrounding tissues.  

(That CO comes from the breakdown of heme proteins in endometrial tissue by heme oxygenase enzymes.  If not immediately excreted, menstrual CO can remain in tissues until perimenopause, when it starts diffusing back out causing hot flashes and other CO symptoms.)

This is easy to see. The CO in menstrual blood causes bright pinkish red color that gets darker as CO decreases.

"Compared with never use or discontinuation of menopausal hormone therapy after age 65 years, the use of estrogen monotherapy beyond age 65 years was associated with significant risk reductions in mortality (19% or adjusted hazards ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.79-0.82), breast cancer (16%), lung cancer (13%), colorectal cancer (12%), congestive heart failure (CHF) (5%), venous thromboembolism (3%), atrial fibrillation (4%), acute myocardial infarction (11%), and dementia (2%). For the use of estrogen and progestogen combo-therapy, both E+ progestin and E+ progesterone were associated with increased risk of breast cancer by 10%-19%, but such risk can be mitigated using low dose of transdermal or vaginal E+ progestin. Moreover, E+ progestin exhibited significant risk reductions in endometrial cancer (45% or adjusted hazards ratio, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.50-0.60), ovarian cancer (21%), ischemic heart disease (5%), CHF (5%), and venous thromboembolism (5%), whereas E+ progesterone exhibited risk reduction only in CHF (4%)."

A cautionary tale, to be sure. However, it suffers from a false assumption when it equates American citizens with Israeli and Russian citizens. Israelis have spent generations surrounded by hostile neighbors and have known war throughout much of their nation's existence. Russians have spent generations under the yoke of authoritarian regimes and know little different.

In other words, citizens of both countries bring vastly different historical experiences to the voting booth than do Americans, who have grown accustomed to exercising freedom of choice in an open, relatively secure environment.

That isn't to suggest that Americans are immune to authoritarianism, particularly in times of uncertainty and stress. But I think there's a fundamental difference between a population with a long tradition of democratic self-government and one whose experience has been shaped by persistent external threats or generations of authoritarian rule. We shouldn't assume that their responses will be the same.

comments.name: Avid Reader

I notice that many people conflate a potential stock market bubble, with AI as a technology.

Some suggest that popping an AI bubble might be beneficial based on the premise that AI is taking replacing workers, consuming resources, etc. In this way, some people seem almost to be rooting for AI companies to fail.

The problem with this is that if there is in fact an AI bubble, and it does indeed pop, it won't change much about AI itself. It will just create widespread economic harm to average people.

When a company goes bankrupt, its product doesn't just disappear. Depending on the type of bankruptcy, the company doesn't even necessarily dissolve at all.

In the case of AI companies, they'll renogotiate data center contracts, or sell off some of those assets. Maybe the company will be bought out by a rival.

But the technology itself will persist. And arguably develop even faster, as the new owners won't be burdened with the legacy debt obligations of the former/defunct company.

When the dot-com bubble burst, the internet didn't go away — the surving companies and technologies went on to redefine the economy, and we are living in that economy to this day, nearly 3 decades later.

AI won't be any different. If OpenAI goes under, their models and assets will simply transfer to new owners. New models will continue to be built. Businesses will still try to replace workers.

But the broader economy will suffer greatly, with ordinary people bearing the brunt of this suffering.

But if yesterday’s huge stock market decline reflects investor concerns that the political shift in Congress and several state governorships will slow AI development and data-center construction, Wall Street has it completely wrong.

In fact, the market should be going through the roof.
For months, we have heard warnings from AI industry employees and some of its most prominent CEOs that AI could become a threat to humanity without meaningful regulation and safeguards. Some have put the risk of AI causing human extinction by the end of the decade at 10 percent.

Investors should pause and reflect on the bigger picture.  Individuals developing this technology are warning us that it could destroy us. Yet Wall Street appears to have a memory issue. Investors appear more concerned about slowing AI development than the risks of allowing it to advance without adequate oversight.

This isn’t about stopping innovation. It’s about keeping AI under human control before it is too late.
America, the world and Wall Street should be celebrating this clear message from American voters: responsible leadership, not Big Tech influence, must help determine our future.  

This is good news for AI and the market, not bad news.

Michael G. Mahoney, Esq.
Centerport, NY

comments.name: Josh
comments.body: Professional mathematician here. This article is bad. Talk to better experts. *Slightly* disproving ETH (emphasis on slight!) is a *world* away from proving P=NP. It's very hard to find serious people who believe P=NP. It's somewhat easier to find people who won't commit. The overwhelming orthodox position remains P != NP. The ETH disproof has basically already been priced in to the community's consensus on these sorts of problems because of OpenAI's similar results from early October proving (*slightly*) sub-n log(n) integer multiplication and DFT algorithms. Those were arguably more shocking. Every asymptotic improvement on these problems for decades has been wildly impractical, with constants so enormous that they're far out of reach of the very finite part of mathematics human civilization occupies in the real world. None of the three results mentioned provide evidence that this pattern will break. All three are enormously interesting intellectually, and one never knows when pure research will make contact with humanity. (AI models themselves are mostly linear algebra on steroids.) But the article draws wild conclusions. Also, the general public has no idea how modern Lean verification works. Every comments section on this sort of article is a mess because of it. The article needs to clarify that the headline result has been formally checked and is effectively certain to be true.

Reads like a modern maritime update to James Michener’s chapter on the Marquis de Rays in Rascals in Paradise.

​In 1879, the Marquis sold European retirees and dreamers a vision of "La Nouvelle-France"—a non-existent South Pacific paradise. People liquidated their life savings for a home that existed only in brochures, only to end up stranded on distant shores when the fragile economics and grand promises inevitably imploded.

​Fast-forward nearly 150 years, and the mechanism remains remarkably identical. Whether it is an uncharted island or an aging ocean liner, selling "escape from reality" as a permanent asset class relies on an illusion of self-containment. 

When fuel prices spike and cash reserves dry up, the romantic pitch collides with hard arithmetic—leaving hopeful buyers stranded thousands of miles from home, holding empty contracts while the company quietly enters restructuring.

​Michener proved that human nature never changes: the urge to buy a ticket to utopia will always exceed the cold calculus of operational reality.

Although the main insurer - Atlantic Mutual - was relatively recently liquidated (2011) and fragmentedly sold to several currently operating insurers, successor ownership of the original owners - White Star Liners - can be much more cleanly stated. 

White Star Lines was bought in part and eventually in entirety between 1934-1950 by Cunard Line. Cunard in turn was bought - again, in part and then eventually in whole - by Carnival Corporation between 1998-1999. Hence Carnival Corporation is the current and sole legal successor to the White Star Liner.

I worked in military intelligence during the Vietnam War.  I know how much can be gleaned from little slip ups and casual conversation.  This should have been an issue that the Trump administration viewed as a potential problem.  There were a number of times where we gleaned solid information from little slip ups.  Our greatest problem was getting the higher ups to take our analysis seriously.   One case in point, we gathered some solid information, in late 1974 that indicated the North Vietnamese would structure a push to take Saigon in the Spring of ‘75.  That combined with some other info convinced us that they would push to take Saigon on May 1st, 1975.  May 1st was a big day in the Communist calendar.  We wrote this up, and sent it up the chain of command.  They didn’t put much faith in what we had put together, and a note came back that Saigon wouldn’t fall on May 1st.

It turns out they were right, Saigon fell to the North Vietnamese on April 30th, not May 1st.  The line I used about this was: “You can lead a person to knowledge but you can’t make them think.”  And, I believe this would apply to Trump and his cronies.

I find it profoundly disturbing that science has become a partisan issue in America. How did we reach a point where accepting scientific evidence is treated as a political position rather than a basic acknowledgment of reality?

Rather than reconcile those beliefs with evidence, they demand that evidence accommodate their faith. And Trump, whose life bears little resemblance to the Christian values his supporters profess to cherish, has been happy to accommodate them.

The consequences extend far beyond the familiar battles over evolution and climate change. We are witnessing political interference in scientific research, the dismantling of institutional expertise, and the erosion of America’s standing as a world leader in discovery and innovation.

Science is not a belief system. It doesn’t require faith, political allegiance, or presidential approval. Its conclusions are subject to evidence, scrutiny, and revision. That is precisely what makes it indispensable.

Religious freedom means Americans are entitled to believe whatever they wish. It does not entitle Christians to impose those beliefs on scientific institutions.

A nation that allows religious dogma and political expediency to dictate the pursuit of science surrenders its intellectual integrity and jeopardizes its future.

Despite being heavily outnumbered and cut off from relief, the Irish held their ground through wave after wave of ground assaults and aerial bombardments. 

The Irish company completely ran out of ammunition, food, and water, and suffered five wounded men. The commandant negotiated a ceasefire and ordered a surrender to save his men from destruction.

Upon returning home, the men faced decades of official indifference, military skepticism, and institutional silence regarding their surrender.

And the cause of a racially-equal, 'race blind' society is not helped by politicians who pander to pretend that embedded, systemic racism is not still present in the United States. Slavery, and the racism generated from it, is the great original sin of the United States, and our political leaders have always been curiously myopic about really seeing it. Even the Founders lofty inspired rhetoric in our founding documents was not backed by the reality of those times. We've seen a systematic effort to roll back the equality laws and protections of the 1960s, always with the pretense that "we're past all that now". So we get school vouchers - though the bigotry that restricts them from madrasas while paying off "Christian" schools is unseen to the politicians who push that out. We get a Supreme Court decision that validates explicitly racial gerrymandering, as long as it's not called that out loud. We continue to have large disparities in minority home ownership, and minority family wealth... all the while being told that we are 'post racial' and that no further improvement is needed. The recent election gives some of the progress towards a more equal society a new chance, but we cannot be complacent about seeking to redress the careful deceit of many of our racially-dividing laws masquerading as 'post racial' protections of freedom.

Most animals, if provided with a stable access to food and a calming, spacious environment can be content to become lifelong 'grazers'.
